query:
Has anyone used tungsten, a tungsten alloy (W-Re, W-La2O3, W-Ni-Fe or W-Ni-Cu heavy alloy) or a
tungsten-coated carbon or graphite part as an ultrasonic sonotrode, horn tip or atomizing plate in
contact with molten metal, especially copper, nickel or copper-nickel alloys (for example in an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another ultrasonic atomizer, or in ultrasonic melt treatment)? If so, report the
melt, temperature, frequency and amplitude, how long the part lasted, how much it eroded or dissolved,
and how much W ended up in the product. If not, give the closest precedents: W or W-coated parts in
contact with molten Cu or Ni alloys (crucibles, nozzles, thermocouple sheaths, casting molds), and Mo
or Nb sonotrodes used with Cu or Ni melts.
task_summary: Report Erosion Contamination And Performance Of Tungsten Sonotrodes With Molten Copper Nickel Alloys

info.name: update_plan
info.description:
Update the plan for a specific or new objective using a JSON string to create or
replace the existing objective.

The updated_json should be a JSON string representing a single plan objective object.

You may use this tool to update an objective, create a new one, or change
strategy if the current plan is not working. Only change strategy significantly
as a last resort, after trying very hard to make the current plan work.

Only mark an objective as completed if you are absolutely sure that it has been fully
met. If it is only partially met, you may add additional objectives to the plan for
what is missing.

plan_objective_id.description: The id of the objective to update.
plan_objective_id.title: Plan Objective Id

updated_plan_objective_json.description:
A JSON string representing the updated objective.
It should be a dictionary with the with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id matching plan_objective_id, if not found, a new objective is created.
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
updated_plan_objective_json.title: Updated Plan Objective Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.
query.title: Query

text_name.description: Name of a text chunk (e.g., 'smith2023example pages 1-5').
text_name.title: Text Name

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available

        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Has anyone used tungsten, a tungsten alloy (W-Re, W-La2O3, W-Ni-Fe or W-Ni-Cu heavy alloy) or a
tungsten-coated carbon or graphite part as an ultrasonic sonotrode, horn tip or atomizing plate in
contact with molten metal, especially copper, nickel or copper-nickel alloys (for example in an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another ultrasonic atomizer, or in ultrasonic melt treatment)? If so, report the
melt, temperature, frequency and amplitude, how long the part lasted, how much it eroded or dissolved,
and how much W ended up in the product. If not, give the closest precedents: W or W-coated parts in
contact with molten Cu or Ni alloys (crucibles, nozzles, thermocouple sheaths, casting molds), and Mo
or Nb sonotrodes used with Cu or Ni melts.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Inconel 718 is a super alloy composed of nickel and chromium, widely used in engineering applications due to its exceptional thermomechanical properties. However, its high work-hardening behavior and low thermal conductivity render conventional machining processes inefficient and challenging, particularly at the microscale. Micro-electrical discharge machining (micro-EDM) has emerged as a promising non-traditional technique for fabricating micro-features in Inconel 718. However, issues continue to arise, including difficulty in maintaining debris evacuation during machining, process stability concerns, and low material removal rates (MRR) and poor surface quality. This review presents micro-EDM of Inconel 718 and the challenges associated with machining using micro-EDM, and then examines how various vibration-assisted strategies have been developed to improve both process stability and efficiency. The review of vibration assist mechanisms on process performance in terms of MRR, total machining time, and surface finish has been discussed. Finally, this review synthesizes the data obtained from the various experiments performed thus far to establish a comprehensive understanding of how vibration assists in stabilizing and increasing the efficiency of the micro-EDM process. Furthermore, while identifying current gaps in the literature, this review suggests potential areas for future development to enhance the process performance and productivity of micro-EDM in micro-scaled machining of Inconel 718.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper possesses exceptional thermal and electrical conductivity, making it valuable in applications ranging from electronics and heat exchangers to aerospace and energy systems. However, its high reflectivity, thermal conductivity, and susceptibility to oxidation present significant challenges in laser additive manufacturing (AM). This review presents a comprehensive overview of the current state of laser AM of copper and copper alloys, with a focus on laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) and laser directed energy deposition (LDED) techniques. The key processing challenges are outlined, including limited laser absorption with infrared lasers, melt pool instability, and porosity formation. Strategies to enhance the processability of copper and its alloys are critically reviewed, including process parameter optimization, material modifications, and the use of alternative laser sources such as green and blue lasers. The role of process monitoring is also discussed as a pathway to ensure process stability and repeatability. The review further highlights recent applications of copper AM and identifies the transition from density-driven optimization to function-oriented qualification as a key requirement for industrial implementation.</jats:p>

Abstract:
This study explores the interfacial friction in ultrasonic micro-injection moulding by using different polymer feedstock shapes, characterisation of micromoulding melts through thermal imaging and assessing microneedle feature replication. Industry standard polypropylene pellets and discs with different thicknesses were used for varying the amount of interfacial friction during sonication. High-speed thermal imaging and tooling containing sapphire windows were used to visualise the melt characteristics. Moulded products were characterised using laser-scanning confocal microscopy to quantify microneedle replication. The study demonstrates that (i) the interfacial area for the different feedstock shapes affects the heating in ultrasonic micro-injection moulding significantly, (ii) disc-shaped feedstocks result in initially higher flow front velocities and exhibit dominance of viscoelastic heating over interfacial friction and (iii) industrial pellet feedstocks provide a good combination interfacial friction and viscoelastic heating and more viscosity reduction in overall leading to better microreplication efficiency. The results presented could have a significant impact on the process development of ultrasonic micro-injection moulding where process repeatability can be improved by controlling the interfacial friction. The research provides an essential contribution to the development of this process, where interfacial frictional heating can be tailored specifically for miniature functional components, offering improved precision and reduced energy use when compared with conventional methods.

Abstract:
Joining processes especially for metallic materials play critical roles in manufacturing industries and structural applications, therefore they are essential to human life. As a more complex technique, under-liquid joining has far-reaching implications for national defense, offshore mining. Furthermore, up-to-now, the effective joining of metals in extreme environments, such as the flammable organo-solvent or the arctic liquid nitrogen, is still uninvestigated. Therefore, an efficient under-liquid joining approach is urgently called for. Here we report a method to join different types of metallic glasses under water, seawater, alcohol and liquid-nitrogen. The dynamic heterogeneity and liquid-like region expansion induces fluid-like behavior under ultrasonic vibration to promote oxide layer dispersion and metal bonding, allowing metallic glasses to be successfully joined in heat-free conditions, while still exhibiting excellent tensile strength (1522 MPa), bending strength (2930 MPa) and improved corrosion properties. Our results provide a promising strategy for manufacturing under offshore, polar, oil-gas and space environments.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Cemented carbides are essential in applications requiring exceptional hardness and wear resistance. However, the reliance on cobalt as a binder raises concerns related to cost, supply security, and health. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are promising cobalt-free binders offering favorable mechanical properties and potential grain-growth control. This work presents a new approach for the development of Co-free WC-based cemented carbide employing an HEA binder designed through CALPHAD-guided simulations. An optimized composition corresponding to Al5Cr5Cu10Fe35Mn10Ni35 (at%) alloy is predicted to be FCC-dominant with minimal σ-phase formation and good compatibility with WC. A preliminary batch of powder of the proposed binder was produced by blending elemental powders, arc remelting, and ultrasonic atomization, yielding predominantly spherical particles with a dendritic microstructure. WC–HEA composites (WC–12 wt% HEA) were then prepared by ball milling, pressing, vacuum sintering, and sinter-HIP for a first evaluation of the microstructure and achievable hardness. The microstructure exhibited residual porosity without significant WC grain coarsening. XRD analyses showed the dominant presence of WC, along with FCC and M3W3C phases (M mainly Fe and Mn), indicating thermal interaction between the binder and WC. Despite these effects, the composite achieved a hardness of 1913 HV and retained a fine WC grain size (0.86 μm). The proposed design approach allowed the definition of a promising Co-free binder composition based on HEA with the expected microstructure, which will need further evaluation, especially aimed at investigating toughness properties as a function of the WC content.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this work, copper–tungsten (Cu-W) composites with a cubic and rhombic dodecahedron W-skeleton were fabricated by the infiltration of Cu melt into a three-dimensionally printed W scaffold. The effects of the skeleton structure on the mechanical properties and energy-absorbing characteristics of the Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composite were investigated and compared with those of commercial Cu-W composite fabricated by powder metallurgy. The results indicated that the mechanical properties of the studied Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composites were mainly related to the properties of their ordered skeletons. Compared to the dodecahedron W-skeleton Cu-W composites, cubic-W-skeleton Cu-W composites exhibited higher strengths but lower absorbed energy. The Cu-W composites with ordered W-skeletons displayed much higher energy absorption than the commercial Cu-W ones. By adjusting the ordered W-skeleton structure contained in the composite, the strength and deformation behavior of the Cu-W composite can be effectively improved, which provides a guide to optimizing the mechanical properties and energy absorption of Cu-W composites.

Abstract:
Copper-based diamond composites have been the focus of many investigations for higher thermal conductivity applications. However, the natural non-wetting behavior between diamond particles and copper matrix makes it difficult to fabricate copper-based diamond composites with high thermal conductivity. Thus, to promote wettability between copper and diamond particles, the copper/diamond interface must be modified by coating alloying elements on the diamond surface or by adding active alloying elements with carbon in the copper matrix. In this paper, we review the research progress on copper-based diamond composites, including theoretical models for calculating the thermal conductivity and the effect of process parameters on the thermal conductivity of copper-based diamond composites. The factors that affect interfacial thermal conductivity are emphatically analyzed in this review. Finally, the current problems of copper-based diamond composites and future research trends are recommended.

From text 'goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 2-4'.

Ivan Goncharov, Vera Popovich, Marcel Sluiter, Anatoly Popovich, and Maurizio Vedani. Design of cobalt-free high-entropy alloy binder for wc-base cemented carbides. Metals, 16:318, Mar 2026. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met16030318, doi:10.3390/met16030318. This article has 1 citations.

The excerpt provides partial information about the tested material in the paper, but not the full patent comparison requested. In the paper, the ultrasonic atomization equipment used a molybdenum sonotrode; tungsten is not identified here as the tested sonotrode material, nor is any proposed tungsten alternative mentioned in the excerpt. The alloy feedstock was based on Al–Cr–Cu–Fe–Mn–Ni: powders of those six elements, each with 99.9% purity and particle sizes below 45 µm, were blended to target compositions, cold pressed, and arc-remelted in water-cooled copper molds before atomization. The atomization platform was an Amazemet rePowder system operated in small batches. The excerpt does not state the melt alloy’s exact final composition, melt or atomization temperature, ultrasonic frequency, sonotrode amplitude, sonotrode lifetime, or tungsten contamination level. It also does not contain the text of US20240390977A1, so patent-specific values and the distinction between a proposed tungsten sonotrode and the material actually tested cannot be established from this excerpt alone. The subsequent WC processing used a WC–12 wt% HEA blend, but this is the powder-processing composition rather than necessarily the atomized melt composition.

## pqac-00000001

From text 'US20240390977A1 pages 4-7'.

Marcin BIELECKI. Method and device for producing heavy metal powders by ultrasonic atomization. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,PL), 2024.

The excerpt establishes that the sonotrode functions as the vibrating anode and is electrically paired with a separate tungsten electrode serving as the cathode. It therefore distinguishes the tungsten electrode from the sonotrode, but it does not identify the actual material of the vibrating sonotrode. The passage also does not provide a numerical ultrasonic frequency, vibration amplitude, sonotrode lifetime, or measured tungsten contamination. It gives an approximate optimum atomization temperature of 1460 K and describes melting heavy-metal feedstock into a molten pool before ultrasonic atomization. The excerpt refers generally to heavy metals and alloys, and the figures mention platinum and CuNi3Si examples, but it does not state a specific melt alloy used in the requested comparison. Consequently, the patent excerpt alone cannot substantiate whether tungsten was proposed as an alternative sonotrode material, what material was tested instead, or the associated lifetime and contamination results. Those details would need to be taken from the fuller patent text and the cited paper, “Design of Cobalt-Free High-Entropy Alloy Binder for WC-Base Cemented Carbides.”

## pqac-00000002

From text 'US20240390977A1 pages 7-9'.

Marcin BIELECKI. Method and device for producing heavy metal powders by ultrasonic atomization. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,PL), 2024.

The excerpt provides only partial information relevant to comparing the patent with the paper. It clearly distinguishes the tungsten component as the electrode/cathode: the arc is formed between the tungsten electrode tip and the sonotrode, while the sonotrode serves as the anode. Therefore, this excerpt does not establish that the tested vibrating sonotrode itself was made of tungsten, nor does it identify an actual sonotrode material or confirm tungsten contamination. The patent describes processing heavy-metal feedstock generally, with examples and discussion involving noble metals such as gold, silver, and copper, but it does not specify the particular melt alloy used in the paper. It gives an atomization-pool temperature range of 2045–2659 K or higher. No sonotrode vibration frequency or amplitude is stated in the supplied pages. Sonotrode lifetime is likewise not quantified; the text only warns that high thermal conductivity can damage the sonotrode and says it must be continuously cooled. Accordingly, the excerpt can support the temperature and electrode-versus-sonotrode distinction, but not the paper’s actual tested material, alloy, frequency, amplitude, lifetime, or W-contamination results, nor the details of any proposed alternative tungsten design.

In this study, the optimization of welding parameters, pore defects, microstructure and mechanical properties of Ti6Al4V alloy welded joints subjected to ultrasonic-assisted laser welding were studied. The optimal parameter combination and the most significant factor influencing the tensile strength of the joint were determined by three-factor and three-level orthogonal experiments with range and variance analysis methods. A control experiment was set up under the optimal parameters to reveal the reason of ultrasonic influence on joint strength from the pore defects and microstructure. The control test showed that the cavitation effect and stirring effect of ultrasonic could significantly improve the weld defects and microstructure. Compared with no ultrasonic, the porosity of the welded joint decreased from 3.06% to 0.08%, and the average grain size of prior-β and α' martensite were refined by 15.1% and 6.7% respectively under an ultrasonic power of 1000W. The ultrasonic vibration also contributed to the grain boundary transformation from low-angle to high-angle and significantly reduced the residual stress inside the joint. With the increase of ultrasonic power, the tensile strength increased by 4.37% and 8.38% respectively and the fracture mode changed from brittle-ductile mixed fracture to ductile fracture.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Welding represents a fundamental metallurgical process that has profoundly transformed modern industry, facilitating the fabrication of intricate structural components, transportation systems, and critical infrastructure. This comprehensive review traces the historical evolution of welding, from early metalworking techniques to contemporary advancements in high-precision, automated methodologies. An in-depth examination of diverse welding techniques including arc welding [Shielded Metal Arc Welding (SMAW), Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW), Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW)], resistance welding, gas welding, and advanced energy beam processes [Laser Beam Welding (LBW), Electron Beam Welding (EBW)] is presented, with a focus on their underlying principles, industrial applications, and technological progressions. Furthermore, solid-state welding processes, such as friction and diffusion welding, are analyzed, underscoring their significance in aerospace, automotive, and high-performance engineering sectors. The study also evaluates prevalent welding defects, quality assessment methodologies (destructive and non-destructive testing), and recent innovations, such as artificial intelligence-driven welding optimization and hybrid welding approaches. With continuous advancements in automation, shielding gas technologies, and real-time monitoring systems, welding remains an indispensable pillar of industrial manufacturing. Future research should prioritize the enhancement of process efficiency, the refinement of weld integrity, and the development of sustainable, high-performance welding solutions to address the evolving demands of modern engineering and fabrication industries.</jats:p>

## pqac-00000008

From text 'US11938557B2 pages 7-10'.

[name redacted]. Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals and a method for processing of liquid …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR,PL), 2024.

The excerpt supports an explicit tungsten-tip test in US11938557B2, rather than merely a candidate-material statement. In the FIG. 8 embodiment, the vibrating working tip is technical-grade tungsten, shaped as a 20 g M8 screw, and contacts the molten Ti7Al6Nb alloy during plasma melting. The sonotrode is a Ti6Al4V body; its measured/identified frequency at 297 K is 20,200 Hz, and the working-tip amplitude is 10 micrometers. The excerpt states that a 3 g Ti7Al6Nb sample is melted using 100 A for 30 seconds, but it does not provide the molten-metal temperature, a quantified tip lifetime, an erosion rate, or measured tungsten contamination. It only says that the tip may degrade and that the diaphragm is then replaced. Tungsten and molybdenum alloys are also listed as suitable high-melting materials for the tip, which is a materials option rather than a separate test. No information about JP7228274B2, W-coated graphite, its molten metal, test temperature, frequency, amplitude, erosion/lifetime, or tungsten contamination appears in this excerpt. Claims/abstract language identifies the tip and sealing arrangement but does not establish testing of every listed material; the detailed tungsten result is the FIG. 8 embodiment.

## pqac-00000009

From text 'US11938557B2 pages 4-7'.

[name redacted]. Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals and a method for processing of liquid …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR,PL), 2024.

The excerpt describes the US patent’s sonotrode as having a vibrating working tip that directly contacts liquid metal, but the detailed embodiment identifies the sonotrode body—and therefore the working-tip structure—as aluminum PA7A, not tungsten, a tungsten alloy, or W-coated graphite. Tungsten and copper alloys appear only as materials an expert might select for other implementations depending on the processed medium; this is a candidate-material statement rather than an explicit tested embodiment. The excerpt gives a nominal ultrasound frequency of 20 kHz and states that the stepped geometry was designed to amplify vibration amplitude four times, but it does not provide a numerical tip amplitude. It also gives an initial dimensional/material condition of 297 K, not a molten-metal processing temperature. No specific molten metal or alloy is identified in this portion beyond general liquid-metal/liquid-alloy processing. No explicit test results for tungsten, tungsten-alloy, or W-coated-graphite tips are reported here, and there are no stated values for lifetime erosion, tungsten contamination, or comparative durability. The excerpt therefore supports distinguishing the aluminum embodiment from tungsten being merely a possible material choice; it supplies no corresponding JP patent evidence.

## pqac-00000010

From text 'US11938557B2 pages 16-18'.

[name redacted]. Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals and a method for processing of liquid …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR,PL), 2024.

The excerpt provides an explicit tested embodiment of US11938557B2 using a technical-grade tungsten working tip, rather than merely listing tungsten as a candidate. The sonotrode body is Grade 5 titanium alloy (Ti6Al4V), while the tip is a 20 g M8 tungsten screw with a semicircular recess. The processed molten metal is a 3 g sample of Ti7Al6Nb alloy, melted by a plasma arc and then subjected to ultrasound. The reported sonotrode frequency is 20,200 Hz at 297 K, and the amplitude at the working tip is 10 micrometers. The cooling liquid is an ethylene-glycol/water mixture at 15°C and 5 L/min; this is a coolant temperature, not the molten-metal temperature. The passage does not report a tip lifetime, measured erosion rate, or tungsten contamination of the alloy. It distinguishes the embodiment from broader disclosure by stating that tungsten or molybdenum alloys are preferable high-melting materials, but the example specifically identifies technical-grade tungsten. The excerpt contains no information about JP7228274B2, W-coated graphite, or comparative tests, so those points cannot be established from this material. It also does not provide claim language or evidence that every claimed embodiment uses tungsten.

## pqac-00000011

From text 'US11938557B2 pages 1-4'.

[name redacted]. Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals and a method for processing of liquid …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR,PL), 2024.

The excerpt identifies tungsten sinters only among preferred high-thermal-conductivity materials discussed for a prior Polish patent application (P.423408), alongside CuCrZr and CuBe. It does not describe an explicit experimental embodiment using a tungsten or tungsten-alloy liquid-metal-contacting vibrating tip, nor does it mention W-coated graphite. The disclosed invention instead emphasizes a sonotrode with a replaceable working tip, which may be made from a material different from the sonotrode body; the tip is the working surface and is treated as a consumable component. The excerpt provides no specific tested tip composition, molten-metal identity, operating temperature, ultrasound frequency, vibration amplitude, erosion lifetime, or tungsten-contamination measurement. It does state general operating constraints: prior systems were limited to approximately 700 °C, and the sonotrode working temperature depends on the processed material’s melting temperature and cooling-system efficiency. The method concerns melting metal on the sonotrode working surface while exciting it mechanically, potentially in an argon-filled vacuum chamber, with electrical heating. These passages therefore support distinguishing candidate material disclosures and structural claims from explicit test data; the supplied pages contain no explicit tungsten performance test or contamination result, and no information about JP7228274B2 is included.

[name redacted]. Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals and a method for processing of liquid …. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,JP,KR,PL), 2024.

The excerpt provides only partial information for US11938557B2 and contains no text from JP7228274B2. In the US patent, tungsten appears as a candidate material in the discussion of an earlier high-temperature sonotrode—“tungsten sinters” are listed alongside CuCrZr and CuBe—not as an explicitly reported tested embodiment in the supplied passage. The claims define a vibrating sonotrode with a working tip for spraying or melting hot material, but do not specify tungsten, a tungsten alloy, or W-coated graphite as the tip material. The excerpt also does not identify a particular molten metal, measured test temperature, amplitude, erosion rate, operating lifetime, or tungsten contamination result. It mentions an approximately 700 °C limitation in the prior-art discussion and claims operation at 16–400 kHz, but these are not presented as a tungsten-tip test dataset. The claims cover alternative tip arrangements, including the sonotrode body itself or a detachable element. Consequently, based solely on this excerpt, tungsten is documented only as a material candidate/reference in the description; no explicit tungsten-tip experiment or associated performance/contamination data can be established. In an embodiment shown in FIGS. 4 a and 4 b , the sonotrode is equipped with a working tip
screwed into the sonotrode body. The working tip may be made from the same material and a
diﬀerent material than the sonotrode body. In a preferable embodiment of the invention, the
working tip is made from high-melting materials, such as tungsten or molybdenum alloys. The
working tip can also act as an element pressing the seal against the sonotrode body, as shown in
FIG. 5 . After the working tip has undergone degradation, the diaphragm is also replaced, which
ensures failure-free sealing. The mass of the working tip 405 preferably does not exceed 0.03 kg
due to the system overload.
Diaphragm 407 could be made of various materials. In lower working temperatures, ﬂuorinated
technopolymer is recommended, e.g. Viton. In the case of higher temperatures, a metal
diaphragm should be used, e.g. made of 316 steel. Preferably, the diaphragm is made of 0.5 mm
thick Ampcoloy 95-copper based material with thermal conductivity above 100 W/mK and
electrical conductivity above 20% IACS, and has a stiﬀness equal to or lower than 10 kN/mm in
the axial direction of the ultrasound system. This allows for heat transfer from the working tip
405 to the cooling liquid to be increased. System sealing takes place directly at the place of
contact of the working tip and the diaphragm. The use of an additional shield 510 is particularly
recommended in higher working temperatures.

same material as the body 104 and the cooling jacket and to ensure the presence of a ﬂexible
elastomer 608 between the seal and the end of the body 104, as shown in FIG. 6 . After the
additional shield 610 is used, the ﬂexible elastomer 608 can be compressed between the seal

present embodiment of the invention, the plate is 1 mm thick—the same as the other jacket
walls. Compression is realized through a plate by cooling liquid pressure. Due to the low plate
thickness, the system is ﬂexible enough not to destroy the polymer seal in low ultrasound

direction. Radial vibrations are also present. In such case, the location of the ﬁrst seal next to

## pqac-00000015

From text 'han2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-5'.

Ying Han, Sida Li, Yu-Tong Cao, Shujun Li, Guangyu Yang, Bo-han Yu, Zhaowei Song, and Jian Wang. Mechanical properties of cu-w interpenetrating-phase composites with different w-skeleton. Metals, 12:903, May 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.3390/met12060903, doi:10.3390/met12060903. This article has 27 citations.

Han et al., “Mechanical properties of Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composites with different W-skeleton” (Metals 12, 903, 2022), reports a direct molten-copper/W contact experiment during composite fabrication. Three-dimensionally printed tungsten scaffolds were placed on blocks of pure copper inside a high-purity graphite crucible. The assembly was heated under flowing argon to 1250 °C at 10 °C/min, held for 10 minutes, and furnace-cooled. The copper melted and infiltrated the porous W scaffold, producing a Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composite. The resulting composite contained 45 vol% W and 63.86 wt% W, with a measured density of 13.5 g/cm³. SEM observations reported that the Cu and W constituents were well combined at the interface, with a steep compositional gradient; the excerpt does not report measurable W dissolution/concentration in the copper, a quantified attack depth, erosion, or interfacial reaction layer. The graphite crucible served as the processing container, rather than the test material. This is therefore evidence of a 1250 °C, 10-minute molten-Cu exposure of W, but it is a fabrication/infiltration study rather than a dedicated long-term crucible, nozzle, mold, or thermocouple-sheath compatibility test. No Cu-Ni, Ni alloy, or W-alloy melt experiment is described in the excerpt.

Abstract:
Tungsten is of industrial relevance due its outstanding intrinsic properties (e.g., highest melting‐point of all elements) and therefore difficult to 3D‐print by conventional methods. Here, tungsten micro‐lattices are produced by room‐temperature extrusion‐based 3D‐printing of an ink comprising WO3–0.5%NiO submicron powders, followed by H2‐reduction and Ni‐activated sintering. The green bodies underwent isotropic linear shrinkage of ≈50% during the thermal treatment resulting in micro‐lattices, with overall 35–60% open‐porosity, consisting of 95–100% dense W–0.5%Ni struts having ≈80–300 μm diameter. Ball‐milling the powders and inks reduced the sintering temperature needed to achieve full densification from 1400 to 1200 °C and enabled the ink to be extruded through finer nozzles (200 μm). Partial sintering of the struts is achieved when NiO is omitted from the ink, with submicron interconnected‐porosity of ≈34%. Several tungsten micro‐lattices are infiltrated with molten copper at 1300 °C under vacuum, resulting in dense, anisotropic W–Cu composites with 40–65% tungsten volume fraction. Partially sintered struts (containing nickel) with submicron open porosity are also infiltrated with Cu, resulting in co‐continuous W–Cu composites with wide W struts/Cu channels at the lattice scale (hundreds of micrometers), and fine W–Cu interpenetrating network at the strut scale (hundreds of nanometers) allowing for the design of anisotropic mechanical and electrical properties.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    GMAW hardfacing with consumables containing tungsten carbides is limited by the dissolution of the carbide particles in the droplet and subsequently in the weld pool. This study investigates the dissolution behavior of unmodified, commercially used eutectoid WC/W
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    C carbides (WSC) and carburized variants (cWSC) featuring a stabilizing WC surface layer under an energy-reduced, controlled short-circuit GMAW hardfacing process. Thermal exposure is considered as two consecutive stages involving dissolution in the molten droplet and diffusion-dominated dissolution during weld-pool residence. Transient electrical process data and weld-pool surface temperature measurements are used to determine the specific droplet enthalpy and the relevant temperature–time regimes. An analytical model based on the shrinking-core concept is developed to quantify carbide dissolution as a function of particle size and cooling time and is validated experimentally by statistical particle-size analysis and particle-counting methods. The results reveal a pronounced size dependence of dissolution, with particles smaller than approximately 80 µm undergoing extensive degradation largely independent of heat input. Carburized carbides exhibit significantly reduced dissolution compared to conventional eutectoid carbides, retaining an intact WC surface layer throughout processing. Furthermore, dissolution is markedly enhanced in iron-based melts compared to iron-nickel systems, indicating that Fe-Ni matrices in combination with carburized carbides are preferable for minimizing carbide degradation in GMAW hardfacing applications.
                  </jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Diamond–copper composites, due to their exceptional thermal conductivity, hold significant potential in the field of electronic device thermal management. Hot-press sintering is a promising fabrication technique with industrial application prospects; however, the thermal conductivity of composites prepared by this method has yet to reach optimal levels. In this study, tungsten was deposited on the surface of diamond particles by magnetron sputtering as an interfacial transition layer, and hot-press sintering was employed to fabricate the composites. The findings reveal that with prolonged annealing time, tungsten gradually transformed into W2C and WC, significantly enhancing interfacial bonding strength. When the diamond volume content was 50% and the interfacial coating consisted of 2 wt.% W, 92 wt.% WC, and 6 wt.% W2C, the composite exhibited a thermal conductivity of 640 W/(m·K), the highest value reported among hot-press sintered composites with diamond content below 50%. Additionally, the AMM (Acoustic Mismatch Model) and DMM (Diffusion Mismatch Model) models were utilized to calculate the interfacial thermal conductance between different phases, identifying the optimal interfacial structure as diamond/W2C/WC/W2C/Cu. This composite material shows potential for application in high-power electronic device cooling, thermal management systems, and thermoelectric conversion, providing a more efficient thermal dissipation solution for related devices.</jats:p>

Abstract:
The pulsed current electrodeposition method was employed for the first time to achieve tungsten coating with a thickness of 433.72 μm on a CuCrZr alloy from Na2WO4-WO3-KCl-NaF molten salt. The microstructure of the coating was observed and the coating density, porosity, hardness, bonding strength, residual stress and oxygen content were tested. The results revealed that the tungsten coating exhibited desirable characteristics such as high density, absence of impurities, excellent adhesion to the matrix (53.16 MPa), residual compressive stress as surface stress, and good stability and durability. Moreover, this thick tungsten coating possesses high density and hardness, low oxygen content and porosity. This offers a novel solution to solve the challenging issue of the connection between tungsten material and heat sink material.

                              that the Cu-W composites with a micro-oriented framework structure had a lower and
                       more stable contact resistance. These studies demonstrate that Cu-W composites with
                        an ordered micro-oriented structure have superior mechanical and electrical properties.
                        However, there are fewer studies on the effects of micro-oriented structural design on the
                          mechanical properties of these composites.
                                 In this work, the Cu-W composites with different ordered skeletons were fabricated
                       by combining the electron beam melting and inﬁltration techniques. Their mechanical
                             properties and energy-absorption characteristics of the composites were investigated, and
                            the underlying mechanism was discussed.

                                   2. Experimental
                                   2.1. Fabrication of W Scaffolds

                          As shown in Figure 1a,b, two kinds of scaffolds with a porosity of 60% were designed
                         with a rhombic dodecahedron and cubic unit cell by Magics, respectively. Tungsten scaf-
                             folds with dimensions of 10 × 10 × 10 mm3 were fabricated by a S150 electron beam
                           melting (EBM) system developed by Xi’an Sailong Metal Materials Co. Ltd. (Xi’an, China).
                         These parts were built layer-by-layer using spherical W powder, with the particle size of
                          15–45 µm. Each layer of powder with thickness of 0.05 mm was laid by raking powder
                              gravity-fed from two cassettes, and preheated to 600 ◦C, then the electron beam melted the
                              selected areas controlled by computer-aided design (CAD). The as-fabricated W scaffolds
                             are shown in Figure 1c and the measured porosity of the studied scaffolds was 55%.Metals 2022, 12, 903                                                                                                             3 of 12





                              Figure 1. Model of the rhombic dodecahedron (a) and cubic (b) scaffolds.  (c) The as-fabricated
               W scaffolds.

                                   2.2. Fabrication of the Cu-W Composites

                           The Cu-W composites were fabricated using the inﬁltration technique. The three-
                            dimensionally (3-D) printed tungsten scaffolds were placed on top of blocks of pure copper
                             in a high-purity graphite crucible. The combination was heated in ﬂowing argon gas
                             to 1250 ◦C, at a heating rate of 10 ◦C/min, held for 10 min, then cooled in a furnace.
                            Before inﬁltration, the copper blocks were mechanically burnished, and then ultrasonically
                           cleaned along with the scaffolds in acetone to reduce contamination. The as-fabricated
                   Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composites are shown in Figure 2. The volume fraction of
             W was 45% and the weight percent was 63.86%. The measured density of the composite
                      was 13.5 g/cm3, which is consistent with that was calculated using the rule-of-mixture.
                       The commercial Cu-W composites with a 60 wt% of W were provided by Shanxi Sirui
                       Advanced Materials Co. Ltd. (Xi’an, China).





                              Figure 2. Macroscopic images of the studied Cu-W composite with cubic (a) and rhombic dodecahe-
                            dron (RD) (b) W-skeleton, and their XRD proﬁles (c).

                                   2.3. Morphologies and Mechanical Properties

                           The microstructure of the studied Cu-W composites was observed by a Tescan Maia
                          3 ﬁeld emission scanning electron microscope (SEM, Tescan Brno, Brno, Czech Republic).
                       The SEM samples were etched by a reagent (10% K3[Fe(CN)6], 10% NaOH, and 80%
                      H2O) for ~30 s. Phase constitutions were examined with the X-ray diffraction (XRD)
                            technique using Cu K irradiation at an accelerating voltage of 40 kV and a current of 250 mA.
                       The rectangular specimens for the compression test were prepared with dimensions of
                          5 mm × 5 mm × 10 mm. According to ASTM E9-2018, compression tests were conducted
                         with an Instron 5869 machine (Norwood, MA, USA) at a strain rate of 8.3 × 10 −3 s−1 at
                      room temperature. The averaged results of two samples were reported for the studied
                            composites.

                                   2.4. Finite Element (FE) Analysis

                            The compressive deformation behavior of the studied composites with different types
                              of skeletons (cubic and rhombic dodecahedron) was simulated using the software packageMetals 2022, 12, 903                                                                                                             4 of 12



                  ABAQUS (ABAQUS 2016, David Hibbitt, Palo Alto, CA, USA). The contact geometric
                       model consisted of a W-skeleton and Cu matrix. The contact relationship between the
                          W-skeleton and Cu matrix was set to bond and maintain the intersection boundary, ﬁx the
                         bottom surface of the contact, and apply compressive stress to the top surface of the contact.
                       The elastic modulus and Poisson’s ratio of Cu used in ABAQUS model were 119 GPa and
                               0.316, respectively, and the elastic modulus and Poisson’s ratio of W were 344 GPa and
                                 0.28, respectively. Every model included 5 mm × 5 mm × 5 unit cells and was divided into
                          approximately ﬁve hundred thousand 10-point tetrahedral elements (C3D10).

                                   3. Experimental Results
                                   3.1. Morphology of the Cu-W Composite

                               Figure 2 shows the macro morphology of the Cu-W composite with ordered W-
                            skeletons prepared in this study, and the corresponding SEM micrographs and XRD pat-
                              terns are shown in Figures 3 and 4. As seen from the ﬁgures, the composite was composed
                             of two kinds of phases, which were orderly arranged. The energy dispersive spectrum
                         (EDS) analysis results (Figures 3 and 4) show that these two kinds of phases were W and
                         Cu, with the W phase having an average thickness of about 800 µm, and Cu and W being
                            orderly arranged in the shape of the cube and rhombic rhombus, respectively. The XRD
                               results indicate that the studied composite mainly consisted of tungsten (body-centered
                            cubic with a = 5.05 Å) and copper (face centered cubic with a = 3.61 Å), and there was
                       no evidence of notable amounts of other phases (Figure 2c). The high-magniﬁcation mor-
                         phology of the interface between the Cu and W showed that the two kinds of constituents
                        were well combined (Figure 5a) and there was a steep component gradient at the interface
                             (Figure 5b,c). In contrast, the arrangement of W and Cu in the commercial Cu-W composites
                      was disordered, not presenting a regular arrangement (Figure 6).





                              Figure 3. SEM micrographs (a) and EDS analysis (b,c) of the Cu-W composite with a cubic-W-skeleton.

      The solubility of tungsten  in liquid nickel,  CH, at 1525~   is 45-46 wt.  % according to
 [i, 2].  At such a high solubility level determiantion of the rate of solution by the rotating
disc method requires preliminary saturation of the melt up to approximately 0.95  c H  [3].
     Experiments have shown that the increase in the concentration of tungsten in nickel
estimated from the loss  in weight of the specimen substantially exceeds the value 0.95 CH,
i.e., the solubility at 1525~  given in  [i, 2]  is low.   Since these authors determined the
solubility  in an unstirred melt,  it may be assumed that a gradient in tungsten concentration
existed along the height of the melt due to an appreciable discrepancy between the density
of liquid nickel and nickel saturated with tungsten.

      In the present work the solubility of tungsten  in liquid nickel was determined by
means of studying the kinetics of solubility  in a melt sitrred under given hydrodynamic con-
ditions.   Electrolytic  nickel  grade N-I (99.98% pure),  0.5 mm thick tungsten sheet (99.95%),
and a single crystal tungsten rod (99.998%) were used.

     Plates of nickel were cut into 20 x i0 mm strips, the surfaces of which were cleaned
of oxide with the aid of grinding paper.   Cylindrical specimens of tungsten I0 mm  in diam-
eter,  60 mm  in length, were prepared from the monocyrystalline tungsten rods (11-16 mm in

from the cylindrical  specimens  after  two,  three,  and four hours  of  i=mlersion proved  that the
minimum  time necessary  to attain equilibrium  was no more than  2 h .

## pqac-00000021

From text 'US20240390977A1 pages 34-36'.

Marcin BIELECKI. Method and device for producing heavy metal powders by ultrasonic atomization. Patent (WO,EP,US,CN,PL), 2024.

The excerpt describes a patent method for ultrasonic atomization of dense, high-melting metals, but it does not report an actual molybdenum or niobium sonotrode experiment, nor does it identify Mo or Nb as the sonotrode material. Copper is included among the potentially atomized metals, and the method is broadly stated to apply to metals with density of at least 8500 kg/m3 and liquidus temperature of at least 1073 K; however, the listed preferred examples do not include molybdenum, niobium, CuNi3Si, nickel, or Cu-Ni-bearing high-entropy alloys. The numerical operating conditions are design limits or proposed adjustable settings rather than documented observations from a completed melt run: ultrasonic transducer power is at least 30 W/cm2 of molten-pool area, frequency is 15–1000 kHz (not Hz), and hot-end vibration velocity is at least 0.2 m/s peak, with droplets up to 100 microns. No operation duration, Mo/Nb dissolution or sonotrode erosion rate, or powder contamination measurement is given. The excerpt therefore cannot substantiate actual Mo/Nb sonotrode treatment of copper-, nickel-, CuNi3Si-, or high-entropy-alloy melts, nor distinguish experimentally measured parameters from patent proposals.

  Heavy Powder Production Systems Based on the Gas Atomization
• EP3216545 describes a production method of powders of noble metals, where the
  atomization process is preferably a gas atomization, a plasma atomization, a centrifugal
  atomization or a crucible-free atomization. As the noble metals' powder application was an
  additive manufacturing, a classiﬁcation on sieves was mandatory after all mentioned types
  of atomization to meet criteria for powder size range. This supplementary classiﬁcation is
  required due to the fact that the gas atomization process results always in the particles
  being in wide range of diameters (usually from 15 to 120 micron in single batch) with
 medium sphericity, while the fractions below 65 microns are produced with yield less 50%
  of the feedstock.
• The additive manufacturing industry expects the powders of premium quality. One of key
  parameter is to obtain a powder of high ﬂowability and this is directly correlated with the
  powder sphericity. Moreover, the maximum diameter of powder (D90) is preferred as low
  as possible from the same reason as well as lower grain size and porosity in ﬁnal product
 made of such powder. Typical 3D printers dedicated to sinter noble metal with low
  roughness of surface ﬁnish require the powders with D90 below 70 microns. On the other
  hand, the very ﬁne powder below 10 microns has poor ﬂowability, what aﬀects adversely
  dispersion of powder onto the bed and in eﬀect 3D printing quality. In order to meet both
  criteria for minimum and maximum powder range, a property like Span is a key metrics to
  qualify a powder batch for the 3D printing application:
• Span = D 90 - D 10 D 50
• The other key property of products sintered of premium alloys (not only 3D printed), it is
  their low porosity, which is function of factors like ﬂowability and low spread between
 minimum and maximum diameter of the powder (preferably D90-D10 <60 micron). The
  ﬂowability is correlated to particle shapes and dry friction against each other. The highest
  and most desirable ﬂowability is obtained for particles as much spherical as possible, what
  can be obtain easily by ultrasonic atomization. The importance of the powder diameter
  spread can be anticipated from FIG. 8 , which shows a correlation of the powder diameter
  range D90-D10 vs. porosity as measured on the 3D printed object made of noble metals.
  The data points collected in FIG. 8 are based on test carried out by D. Maier and S. Humm
  for Heraeus Deutschland GmbH on materials: pure iridium, silver, gold, Pt80Ru20 and
  Pt50Ru50 alloys, after sintering with same parameters by a selective laser melting (SLM)
  technique on the machine Conceptlaser, model MLab. The porosity here were calculated
  based on sample density. To summarize, ultrasonic atomization of metals and their alloys
   is the most suitable method of metal atomization regarding quality of the powders, namely
  span and sphericity of particles. An additionally further classiﬁcation process can be
  applied on request. However, for most applications the powders obtained by the ultrasonic
  atomization are already of very good quality allowing direct usage e.g. in additive
  manufacturing without subsequent sieve classiﬁcation in the integrated system.
• This is why in the past a device and a method for ultrasonic atomization was developed by  the Applicant (see WO2019/092641 A1) to produce the powders made of typical structural
  alloys available commercially e.g. stainless steel, Inconel (Ni-based) or titanium alloys.
  However, said known device and method for ultrasonic atomization is not eﬃcient to
  produce heavy and noble metal powders of satisfactory quality as reached for above
  typical structural alloys.
• To highlight the essentials of the ultrasonic atomization is, one can compare these
  structural alloys to pure heavy elements or their alloys, preferably noble metals, due to the
  fact the steel as well as Ni-/Ti-/Co-based alloys present other-easier for processing at high
  temperature-material properties, like:
  ○  ■ lower density, what means that less energy is needed to melt and then eject
             droplets from molten metal pool,
     ■ lower reﬂectivity for the radiation in infrared wavelength, what is very
            beneﬁcial during heating by the electric arc or laser beam,
     ■ lower melting temperature and concurrently enthalpy, which are important for
            energy eﬃciency of entire atomization process,
     ■ usually lower thermal and electrical conductivity, what exaggerate a thermal
             gradient in the molten metal pool, if heated by the electric arc,
     ■ lower surface tension for alloys than pure elements, what is a desirable
            property in order to reduce the powder mean particle size (D50) and energy
           consumption for droplets formation.

  powders according will be described for two diﬀerent embodiments, the ﬁrst named
  hereinafter “in vacuum”, the second one named “with gas”. The term “in vacuum” is used
  here as meaning conditions in which the chamber 2′ (called hereinafter the vacuum

  (chemically inert) at pressure in the range 0.01 to 6 barA, but preferably 1-1.5 barA.

  the invention begins by a step 100 of providing a heavy metal raw material 5 in the
  vicinity of a heat source 13. The raw material 5 is preferably in the form of a wire or rod,

  to heat up from the ambient temperature at supply conditions and then changes its state to
  a liquid one. As a result, a molten metal is formed within the molten metal pool 21.

  to utilize as the heat source 13 an electric arc between a cathode and an anode. The
  cooled cathode 6 can be armed with a non-consumable tungsten electrode 23, while the
  anode can concurrently work as a vibration source, namely a sonotrode 3, which is also
  able to conduct electricity. Melting takes place on the sonotrode 3, namely in the molten

  the surface of the molten metal pool 21 is around 1.3 times of its melting temperature,
  however in general the temperature on the surface of the molten metal pool 21 has a
  temperature equal to or greater than the melting temperature (liquidus) of the heavy metal
  raw material 5, but below the vaporization temperature of the atomized heavy metal raw

  heavy metals, particularly noble elements. The best pressure level from above range
  should be identiﬁed for each processed heavy metal composition in following steps:  ○  ■ a. Select optimal atomization temperature to reach eﬃcient powder output
             (usually ˜1.3 times of meting temperature in deg K);
     ■ b. Check the vapor pressure at above optimal atomization temperature for the
           molten metal (material property to be found in handbooks);
     ■  c. Set-up the chamber pressure with aid of vacuum pump at level equal to the
            vapor pressure from previous point.

ABSTRACT
Abstract

A device for production of heavy metal powders by ultrasonic atomization from a heavy metal
raw material is provided. The device comprises a feeding means, a heat source, an adjustingmeans, and a collecting means. The feeding provides the heavy metal raw material in the
vicinity of the heat source, and the heat source generates an electric arc to heat the heavy metal
raw material to create a molten metal pool on a sonotrode. The sonotrode provides ultrasonic
mechanical vibrations to the molten metal pool to cause heavy metal droplets to be ejected from
the molten metal pool. The adjusting means adjusts the feeding means, the heating means, and
the sonotrode to direct the heavy metal droplets to cause the heavy metal droplets to freely cool
down within a predetermined distance and transform the heavy metal droplets to the heavy
metal powder.
CLAIMS
Claims (19)

What is claimed is:
1. A device for production of heavy metal powders by ultrasonic atomization from a heavy
metal raw material that comprises an electrically conductive metal having a density>8500 kg/
m3 and a melting temperature (liquidus)>1073 deg K=800 C at 1 barA, the device comprising:
feeding means for providing the heavy metal raw material in the vicinity of a heat source;
wherein the heat source has an electrode and generates an electric arc to heat the heavy metal
raw material so as to create a molten metal pool on a sonotrode, wherein the molten metal pool
has a temperature equal to or greater than the melting temperature of the heavy metal raw
material, wherein the molten metal pool has a temperature below a vaporization temperature of
the heavy metal raw material, and wherein the sonotrode provides ultrasonic mechanical
vibrations to the molten metal pool, so as to cause heavy metal droplets to be ejected from the
molten metal pool;
an adjusting means comprising at least one processor and at least one memory and conﬁgured to
adjust feeding means parameters of the feeding means, adjust heating means parameters of the
heating means, and adjust sonotrode parameters of the sonotrode to direct the heavy metal
droplets away from the molten metal pool, so as to cause the heavy metal droplets to freely cool
down at least by radiation within a predetermined distance and transform the heavy metal
droplets to the heavy metal powder;
collecting means for collecting the heavy metal powder;
wherein the electrode is a cathode;
wherein the sonotrode is an anode;
wherein the electric arc is of the length in the range from 5 mm to 40 mm;
wherein the electric arc length is measured between a tip of the cathode and a center of the
sonotrode;
wherein a power supplied to the electric arc does not exceed 15 KW per 1cm2 of the area of the
molten metal pool;
