Keywords: aluminium alloy; alumina; nanoparticles; ultrasonic treatment; plastic deformation; residual porosity 1. Introduction The development of the aerospace and automotive industry is accompanied by an increase in the requirements for the materials, primarily by high specific strength and workability at low cost [1]. Traditional aluminium alloys do not fully satisfy the requirements. In this regard, at present, the development of new lightweight metal materials with the required characteristics is being actively pursued. One of the trends in the development of advanced materials is metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced by refractory, mainly ceramic particles [2–4]. The manufacturing of the materials is possible by different methods; however, casting technologies are the most universal and efﬁcient method [2,4]. At the same time, the production of bulk ingots of the composite materials by casting is associated with a number of problems caused by the agglomeration and ﬂotation of particles. This phenomenon is observed due to poor melt wettability of the reinforcing particles [5]. As a result, a reduced density is observed in composites due to the residual porosity, decreasing their mechanical characteristics [6]. There are several solutions to the problem: applying coatings on the particles that increase wettability, using master alloys, and/or imposing external ﬁelds on the metallic melt [3–7]. In this study, a specially prepared master alloy as well as ultrasonic treatment of the melt was used. As shown elsewhere [8], the presence of dispersed particles in metallic materials can lead to refining the grain structure when processed by the methods of severe plastic deformation. In addition, Metals 2017, 7, 544; doi:10.3390/met7120544 www.mdpi.com/journal/metalsMetals 2017, 7, 544 2 of 7 this treatment allows reduced residual porosity in powder materials [9]. At the same time, such studies have not been conducted to-date for the metal matrix aluminium-based composites produced by casting. Severe plastic deformation is also limited to relatively small samples and requires specialized equipment. This work focuses on the effects of combined helical and pass rolling on the structure, residual porosity, and microhardness of a composite based on an AA6082 aluminium alloy with small additions of Al2O3 (0.2 wt %) nanoparticles. The nanoparticles are obtained by casting using pre-prepared master alloys and ultrasonic processing. The choice of alumina Al2O3 as reinforcing particles is observed because they have a signiﬁcantly higher strength and hardness, as well as chemical and thermal stability compared to aluminium [10]. 2. Materials and Methods An AA6082-grade aluminium alloy (Al-1Si-0.9Mg-0.7Mn-0.5Fe-0.1Cu-0.25Cr-0.2Zn-0.1Ti) was used as the initial material. To obtain a master alloy, the powder of aluminium oxide (particle size <100 nm) was obtained by the electric explosion of wire. Aluminium powder with particles less than 50 µm were used [3]. A powder mixture of Al and 5 wt % Al2O3 was prepared. For de-agglomeration and uniform distribution of the nanoparticles in the powder mixture, stirring was performed using stearic acid as a surfactant. Next, 200 mL of petroleum ether and 1.5 wt % of stearic acid were added to the powder mixture. After that step, mechanical stirring of the powder mixture was carried out for 20 min, followed by drying in air and sieving. To obtain the master alloy from this powder mixture, a shock-wave compacting method was used. A detailed scheme of the method of shock-wave compacting of powder mixtures can be found elsewhere [3]. The AA6082 alloy was melted in a graphite crucible with a total volume of melt 500 g. Ultrasonic processing was carried out using a 5-kW water-cooled magnetostrictive transducer (RELTECH, Sankt-Peterburg, Russia) at an operating frequency of 17.5 kHz. A conical sonotrode with a working amplitude of ~30 µm was made from niobium. Ultrasonic degassing was carried out at a melt temperature of 730 ◦C for 1 min. The Al-5 wt % Al2O3 master alloy in the form of a rod was introduced in the area of ultrasonic cavitation in the melt directly under the sonotrode. After the master alloy was introduced, the melt was further treated with ultrasound for 2 min at a temperature of 730 ◦C. Next, the melt was poured into a steel mould with an inner diameter of 25 mm at a temperature of 710 ◦C. The nominal content of alumina nanoparticles in the composite was 0.2 wt %. Additionally, for comparison, a matrix alloy without Al2O3 particles proceeded following the same schedule. The deformation processing of cast billets was performed by a combination of helical and pass rolling. Helical rolling was conducted in a mini rolling mill “14–40”. Before the first rolling, the billet with a diameter of 25 mm was heated to a temperature of 420 ◦C for 20 min. Between the next passes, the billet was held in a furnace at a temperature of 420 ◦C for 5 min. The total deformation was approximately ~32%. Further deformation was carried out in a rolling mill with pass rolls at room temperature. As a result of such rolling, we received bars of square section 10 mm × 10 mm. The total accumulated deformation amounted to ~80%, which corresponds to the true logarithmic strain e ~1.6 [11]. Figure 1 demonstrates the processing scheme of combined rolling. The structure was studied by optical metallography (OM, Olympus, Tokyo, Japan) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM, FEI Company, Hillsboro, OR, USA) with electron diffraction of back scattered electrons (EBSD). The surface of the samples for OM and EBSD analysis were prepared by mechanical grinding and electrolytic polishing. **Yes—but the documented tungsten sonotrode tip was used with a titanium alloy, not a copper or nickel melt.** A patent describes a technical-grade tungsten working tip that supports molten Ti7Al6Nb and transmits ultrasound. I found **no verified report of a tungsten, W–Re, W–La₂O₃, W–Ni–Fe or W–Ni–Cu tip, or a tungsten-coated carbon/graphite tip, operating against molten Cu, Ni or Cu–Ni** with measured service life, erosion and W pickup. This is a limit of the located evidence, not proof that no such equipment has ever been used. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000036)

| Precedent and evidential status | Melt and conditions | Lifetime, loss and product contamination |
|---|---|---|
| **W tip, explicit patent embodiment:** [name redacted], *Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals*, US11938557B2. A 20-g, technical-grade W M8 working tip is attached to a Ti6Al4V sonotrode body and contacts the melt. | A **3-g Ti7Al6Nb** charge is melted with a **100-A plasma arc for 30 s**; the arc is then extinguished and ultrasound applied. The assembly’s frequency is **20,200 Hz measured at 297 K**—not a stated frequency measured at melt temperature—and tip amplitude is **10 µm**. Melt temperature and duration of subsequent sonication are **not given**. | **No quantified lifetime, recession, mass loss or W concentration** in the treated alloy. The patent contemplates replacing a tip after degradation, but supplies no wear measurement. This is a disclosed worked example, **not** a published Cu/Ni durability trial. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014) |
| **Mo tip, reported rePowder processing:** Goncharov *et al.*, *Metals* **16**, 318 (2026), doi:10.3390/met16030318. | An **AMAZEMET rePowder** with a **molybdenum sonotrode** atomizes an Al–Cr–Cu–Fe–Mn–Ni high-entropy-alloy feedstock prepared from elemental powders and arc-remelted rods. This is a **Cu- and Ni-containing alloy**, not pure Cu or a conventional Cu–Ni alloy. The accessible methods give **no atomization temperature, frequency or amplitude**; temperatures given for later WC–HEA sintering are not melt-atomization temperatures. | **No tip operating life, erosion/dissolution rate or W pickup** reported. The subsequent **WC–12 wt% HEA** mixture contains deliberately added WC and must not be interpreted as W contamination from the Mo sonotrode. (pqac-00000004) |
| **CuNi3Si atomization, vibrating material unspecified:** Bielecki, US20240390977A1. | The patent expressly reports **CuNi3Si powder made at 35 kHz** using a cooled sonotrode in argon; it gives feedstock **liquidus 1348 K (≈1075 °C)**, **not a measured operating melt temperature**. Its tested apparatus has a **3-mm tungsten arc cathode separate from the vibrating sonotrode/anode**. It reports an experimental hot-end vibration-*velocity* threshold of **0.2 m/s peak**, not the actual displacement amplitude for this CuNi3Si run. | The patent says sonotrodes are exchanged when contaminated by a previous feedstock, but gives **neither tip composition nor service life, erosion or product W assay**. Thus its W electrode cannot establish a W sonotrode or W-derived powder contamination. (pqac-00000027, pqac-00000028) |
| **Nb-tip design, not a Cu/Ni performance test:** Kaczynski *et al.*, EP3766610A1. | An atomizing-sonotrode embodiment has a **niobium core pressed into a copper-alloy body**; W and Mo alloys are listed as *alternative* core materials. It describes possible installation for steels and Ti alloys, but gives **no identified Cu/Ni melt run, test temperature, measured frequency or amplitude** for its Nb embodiment. | **No measured life, wear or contamination.** The coating specified on the *coolant-side body* is for protection against cooling-liquid cavitation, not a W coating on graphite exposed to metal. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036) |
| **Nb immersed-sonotrode experiment, lower-temperature comparator:** Naydenkin *et al.*, *Metals* **7**, 544 (2017), doi:10.3390/met7120544. | **AA6082 aluminum alloy** at **730 °C**, **17.5 kHz**, approximately **30 µm** working amplitude. A niobium conical sonotrode was used for **1 min** of degassing and **2 additional min** after addition of Al–Al₂O₃ master alloy. | Three minutes describes **one treatment schedule, not demonstrated tip life**. Nb wear and pickup are not quantified. The alloy’s minor nominal Cu content does not make this a molten-copper trial. (pqac-00000038) |

**Closest non-ultrasonic W–melt-contact evidence.** Pure Cu infiltrated W scaffolds at **1250 °C for 10 min** under argon in Han *et al.*; interfacial microscopy found distinct, bonded Cu and W constituents, but neither W loss nor W dissolved in the Cu was measured. Calvo *et al.* similarly infiltrated W microlattices with Cu at **1200 or 1300 °C for 60 min** in vacuum. These are stationary, short-duration composite-fabrication exposures—not qualifying crucible, nozzle, mold, sheath or cavitating-tip lifetime tests. (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000031)

Nickel presents a particularly strong **chemical-dissolution warning**. Natanzon *et al.*, *Soviet Powder Metallurgy and Metal Ceramics* **31**, 161–165 (1992), doi:10.1007/BF00794054, measured **50.7 ± 1.4 wt% equilibrium W solubility in stirred liquid Ni at 1525 °C**; W specimens were immersed for **2–4 h** to establish equilibrium. Their rotating-disc tests measured dissolution over **270–720 s**, with solution-rate constants dependent on rotation. This is a deliberately dissolving stationary/rotating W specimen, **not an ultrasonic wear rate or a predicted W concentration in atomized powder**. That paper also cites Eremenko, Minakova and Churakov, “Solubility of tungsten in cupro-nickel melts,” *Poroshkovaya Metallurgiya*, no. 4, 53–58 (1977); I could verify the citation **but not obtain its Cu–Ni-specific numerical results**. (pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020)

**Bottom line for the requested metrics:** The titanium-alloy patent supplies the sole located explicit molten-metal-contact **W vibrating-tip** configuration and its frequency/amplitude, but **not its melt temperature, tip life, loss or W pickup**. The Mo/rePowder paper and 35-kHz CuNi3Si patent establish substantially closer **Cu/Ni-containing ultrasonic-processing** precedents, but do **not** establish a W sonotrode or quantify its contamination. I found no defensible numerical W-in-product value or service-life estimate for a W, W-alloy or W-coated-graphite sonotrode in molten Cu/Ni; neither the short stationary Cu exposures nor Ni equilibrium solubility can be substituted for those measurements. (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000028, pqac-00000016, pqac-00000018)"}

Introduction The development of the aerospace and automotive industry is accompanied by an increase in the requirements for the materials, primarily by high specific strength and workability at low cost [1]. Traditional aluminium alloys do not fully satisfy the requirements. In this regard, at present, the development of new lightweight metal materials with the required characteristics is being actively pursued. One of the trends in the development of advanced materials is metal matrix composites (MMCs) reinforced by refractory, mainly ceramic particles [2–4]. The manufacturing of the materials is possible by different methods; however, casting technologies are the most universal and efﬁcient method [2,4]. At the same time, the production of bulk ingots of the composite materials by casting is associated with a number of problems caused by the agglomeration and ﬂotation of particles. This phenomenon is observed due to poor melt wettability of the reinforcing particles [5]. As a result, a reduced density is observed in composites due to the residual porosity, decreasing their mechanical characteristics [6]. There are several solutions to the problem: applying coatings on the particles that increase wettability, using master alloys, and/or imposing external ﬁelds on the metallic melt [3–7]. In this study, a specially prepared master alloy as well as ultrasonic treatment of the melt was used. As shown elsewhere [8], the presence of dispersed particles in metallic materials can lead to refining the grain structure when processed by the methods of severe plastic deformation. In addition, Metals 2017, 7, 544; doi:10.3390/met7120544 www.mdpi.com/journal/metalsMetals 2017, 7, 544 2 of 7 this treatment allows reduced residual porosity in powder materials [9]. At the same time, such studies have not been conducted to-date for the metal matrix aluminium-based composites produced by casting. Severe plastic deformation is also limited to relatively small samples and requires specialized equipment. This work focuses on the effects of combined helical and pass rolling on the structure, residual porosity, and microhardness of a composite based on an AA6082 aluminium alloy with small additions of Al2O3 (0.2 wt %) nanoparticles. A powder mixture of Al and 5 wt % Al2O3 was prepared. For de-agglomeration and uniform distribution of the nanoparticles in the powder mixture, stirring was performed using stearic acid as a surfactant. Next, 200 mL of petroleum ether and 1.5 wt % of stearic acid were added to the powder mixture. After that step, mechanical stirring of the powder mixture was carried out for 20 min, followed by drying in air and sieving. To obtain the master alloy from this powder mixture, a shock-wave compacting method was used. A detailed scheme of the method of shock-wave compacting of powder mixtures can be found elsewhere [3]. Ultrasonic processing was carried out using a 5-kW water-cooled magnetostrictive transducer (RELTECH, Sankt-Peterburg, Russia) at an operating frequency of 17.5 kHz. **Yes—but the documented tungsten sonotrode tip was used with a titanium alloy, not a copper or nickel melt.** A patent describes a technical-grade tungsten working tip that supports molten Ti7Al6Nb and transmits ultrasound. I found **no verified report of a tungsten, W–Re, W–La₂O₃, W–Ni–Fe or W–Ni–Cu tip, or a tungsten-coated carbon/graphite tip, operating against molten Cu, Ni or Cu–Ni** with measured service life, erosion and W pickup. This is a limit of the located evidence, not proof that no such equipment has ever been used. (US11938557B2 pages 7-10, US11938557B2 pages 16-18, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42, EP3766610A1 pages 2-8)

| Precedent and evidential status | Melt and conditions | Lifetime, loss and product contamination |
|---|---|---|
| **W tip, explicit patent embodiment:** [name redacted], *Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals*, US11938557B2. A 20-g, technical-grade W M8 working tip is attached to a Ti6Al4V sonotrode body and contacts the melt. | A **3-g Ti7Al6Nb** charge is melted with a **100-A plasma arc for 30 s**; the arc is then extinguished and ultrasound applied. The assembly’s frequency is **20,200 Hz measured at 297 K**—not a stated frequency measured at melt temperature—and tip amplitude is **10 µm**. Melt temperature and duration of subsequent sonication are **not given**. | **No quantified lifetime, recession, mass loss or W concentration** in the treated alloy. The patent contemplates replacing a tip after degradation, but supplies no wear measurement. This is a disclosed worked example, **not** a published Cu/Ni durability trial. (US11938557B2 pages 7-10, US11938557B2 pages 16-18) |
| **Mo tip, reported rePowder processing:** Goncharov *et al.*, *Metals* **16**, 318 (2026), doi:10.3390/met16030318. | An **AMAZEMET rePowder** with a **molybdenum sonotrode** atomizes an Al–Cr–Cu–Fe–Mn–Ni high-entropy-alloy feedstock prepared from elemental powders and arc-remelted rods. This is a **Cu- and Ni-containing alloy**, not pure Cu or a conventional Cu–Ni alloy. The accessible methods give **no atomization temperature, frequency or amplitude**; temperatures given for later WC–HEA sintering are not melt-atomization temperatures. | **No tip operating life, erosion/dissolution rate or W pickup** reported. The subsequent **WC–12 wt% HEA** mixture contains deliberately added WC and must not be interpreted as W contamination from the Mo sonotrode. (goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 2-4) |
| **CuNi3Si atomization, vibrating material unspecified:** Bielecki, US20240390977A1. | The patent expressly reports **CuNi3Si powder made at 35 kHz** using a cooled sonotrode in argon; it gives feedstock **liquidus 1348 K (≈1075 °C)**, **not a measured operating melt temperature**. Its tested apparatus has a **3-mm tungsten arc cathode separate from the vibrating sonotrode/anode**. It reports an experimental hot-end vibration-*velocity* threshold of **0.2 m/s peak**, not the actual displacement amplitude for this CuNi3Si run. | The patent says sonotrodes are exchanged when contaminated by a previous feedstock, but gives **neither tip composition nor service life, erosion or product W assay**. Thus its W electrode cannot establish a W sonotrode or W-derived powder contamination. (US20240390977A1 pages 38-40, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42) |
| **Nb-tip design, not a Cu/Ni performance test:** Kaczynski *et al.*, EP3766610A1. | An atomizing-sonotrode embodiment has a **niobium core pressed into a copper-alloy body**; W and Mo alloys are listed as *alternative* core materials. It describes possible installation for steels and Ti alloys, but gives **no identified Cu/Ni melt run, test temperature, measured frequency or amplitude** for its Nb embodiment. | **No measured life, wear or contamination.** The coating specified on the *coolant-side body* is for protection against cooling-liquid cavitation, not a W coating on graphite exposed to metal. (EP3766610A1 pages 1-2, EP3766610A1 pages 2-8) |
| **Nb immersed-sonotrode experiment, lower-temperature comparator:** Naydenkin *et al.*, *Metals* **7**, 544 (2017), doi:10.3390/met7120544. | **AA6082 aluminum alloy** at **730 °C**, **17.5 kHz**, approximately **30 µm** working amplitude. A niobium conical sonotrode was used for **1 min** of degassing and **2 additional min** after addition of Al–Al₂O₃ master alloy. | Three minutes describes **one treatment schedule, not demonstrated tip life**. Nb wear and pickup are not quantified. The alloy’s minor nominal Cu content does not make this a molten-copper trial. (naydenkin2017influenceofcombined pages 1-3) |

**Closest non-ultrasonic W–melt-contact evidence.** Pure Cu infiltrated W scaffolds at **1250 °C for 10 min** under argon in Han *et al.*; interfacial microscopy found distinct, bonded Cu and W constituents, but neither W loss nor W dissolved in the Cu was measured. Calvo *et al.* similarly infiltrated W microlattices with Cu at **1200 or 1300 °C for 60 min** in vacuum. These are stationary, short-duration composite-fabrication exposures—not qualifying crucible, nozzle, mold, sheath or cavitating-tip lifetime tests. (han2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-5, calvo2018microstructureandprocessing pages 2-3)

Nickel presents a particularly strong **chemical-dissolution warning**. Natanzon *et al.*, *Soviet Powder Metallurgy and Metal Ceramics* **31**, 161–165 (1992), doi:10.1007/BF00794054, measured **50.7 ± 1.4 wt% equilibrium W solubility in stirred liquid Ni at 1525 °C**; W specimens were immersed for **2–4 h** to establish equilibrium. Their rotating-disc tests measured dissolution over **270–720 s**, with solution-rate constants dependent on rotation. This is a deliberately dissolving stationary/rotating W specimen, **not an ultrasonic wear rate or a predicted W concentration in atomized powder**. That paper also cites Eremenko, Minakova and Churakov, “Solubility of tungsten in cupro-nickel melts,” *Poroshkovaya Metallurgiya*, no. 4, 53–58 (1977); I could verify the citation **but not obtain its Cu–Ni-specific numerical results**. (natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 1-2, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 2-4, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 4-5)

**Bottom line for the requested metrics:** The titanium-alloy patent supplies the sole located explicit molten-metal-contact **W vibrating-tip** configuration and its frequency/amplitude, but **not its melt temperature, tip life, loss or W pickup**. The Mo/rePowder paper and 35-kHz CuNi3Si patent establish substantially closer **Cu/Ni-containing ultrasonic-processing** precedents, but do **not** establish a W sonotrode or quantify its contamination. I found no defensible numerical W-in-product value or service-life estimate for a W, W-alloy or W-coated-graphite sonotrode in molten Cu/Ni; neither the short stationary Cu exposures nor Ni equilibrium solubility can be substituted for those measurements. (US11938557B2 pages 16-18, goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 2-4, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42, han2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-5, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 1-2)

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns computational phase-stability and composition optimization of cobalt-free high-entropy-alloy binders for WC-base cemented carbides. It does not provide the ultrasonic-atomization patent’s equipment details or identify an actual vibrating sonotrode material, tested melt alloy, processing temperature, frequency, amplitude, sonotrode lifetime, or tungsten contamination. In the paper, the initial Co-free alloy considered was Al0.5CrCuFeMnNi. Elemental trends were evaluated: increasing Cr promotes BCC and SIGMA phases, whereas increasing Fe or Ni promotes FCC and suppresses BCC/SIGMA; Al was kept below equiatomic content because it strongly stabilizes BCC. Optimization produced several candidate compositions, including Al0.5CrCuFeMnNi, Al0.5CrCuFeMnNi2 (HEA 2-1), Al8.3Cr8.3Cu16.1Fe16.1Mn16.1Ni35 (HEA 2-2), and AlCr5Cu12Fe23Mn20Ni35 (HEA 2-3). The target was an FCC-dominant binder, because FCC compositions are associated with higher toughness, while minimizing SIGMA and maintaining stability with WC. Therefore, this excerpt cannot distinguish a proposed alternative tungsten sonotrode from the material actually tested; those facts would need to be taken from the patent and other sections of the paper.

It identifies the sonotrode as the vibrating, electrically conductive anode and states that melting occurs on its surface in the molten-metal pool. Tungsten is explicitly associated with the separate, non-consumable cathode electrode, not with the sonotrode: the arc is formed between the tungsten electrode tip (cathode) and the sonotrode (anode). The passage does not disclose the sonotrode’s actual material, the specific melt alloy tested, ultrasonic frequency, vibration amplitude, sonotrode lifetime, or tungsten contamination measurements. It also does not establish whether tungsten was the tested sonotrode material or merely a proposed alternative. The only quantified process conditions here concern the electric arc and atmosphere: low-voltage electricity of 10–40 V, a 5–40 mm arc length in the gas embodiment, and atomization temperatures generally at or above the alloy liquidus and preferably about 1.3 times the melting temperature. Those values should not be substituted for ultrasonic operating frequency or amplitude. Additional passages from the patent and the cited paper are required to identify the tested sonotrode composition and compare it with any tungsten alternative.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides only general conclusions and descriptions of proposed testing, not the specific experiments requested. It states that refractory metals, including tungsten and tungsten alloys, exhibited low solubility under pyrochemical process conditions and that tungsten was nearly corrosion resistant in the cited tests. The test sequence included an isothermal capsule test, corrosion agitator test, crucible test, solution stability test, thermal convection loop test, and prototype vessel testing, but this passage does not identify which tests used molten copper, copper–nickel, or nickel alloys in contact with tungsten. It also gives no melt compositions, temperatures, exposure times, measured tungsten concentrations, or quantified attack rates. The passage does mention graphite molds and reports that metal–mold interaction during tungsten casting was severe, requiring removal of 0.32–0.48 cm of surface material, but it does not establish that the interacting melt was copper, copper–nickel, or a nickel alloy, nor does it describe tungsten coating on graphite in such a melt. Thus, the excerpt can support only broad claims about tungsten’s reported corrosion resistance and the existence of crucible-related testing; it cannot substantiate any qualifying experiment under the question’s required reporting criteria.

contexts.context: Han et al., “Mechanical properties of Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composites with different W-skeleton” (Metals 12, 903, 2022), reports a direct molten-copper/W contact experiment during composite fabrication. Three-dimensionally printed tungsten scaffolds were placed on blocks of pure copper inside a high-purity graphite crucible. The assembly was heated under flowing argon to 1250 °C at 10 °C/min, held for 10 minutes, and furnace-cooled. The copper melted and infiltrated the porous W scaffold, producing a Cu-W interpenetrating-phase composite. The resulting composite contained 45 vol% W and 63.86 wt% W, with a measured density of 13.5 g/cm³. SEM observations reported that the Cu and W constituents were well combined at the interface, with a steep compositional gradient; the excerpt does not report measurable W dissolution/concentration in the copper, a quantified attack depth, erosion, or interfacial reaction layer. The graphite crucible served as the processing container, rather than the test material. This is therefore evidence of a 1250 °C, 10-minute molten-Cu exposure of W, but it is a fabrication/infiltration study rather than a dedicated long-term crucible, nozzle, mold, or thermocouple-sheath compatibility test. No Cu-Ni, Ni alloy, or W-alloy melt experiment is described in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports rotating tungsten-disc dissolution experiments in liquid nickel, not ultrasonic atomization or sonotrodes. At 1525°C, angular velocities were 4.45–36.8 rad/s; tungsten dissolution rate constants were \(0.77\pm0.15\), \(1.57\pm0.26\), \(1.95\), and \(3.72\) × \(10^{-4}\) m/s, respectively. For 4.45–25 rad/s, \(K=(3.47\pm0.04)\times10^{-5}\omega^{0.58\pm0.02}\), indicating diffusion-controlled dissolution; the calculated W diffusion coefficient was \((1.41\pm0.07)\times10^{-8}\) m²/s. No erosion duration, dissolved mass, resulting product W, ultrasonic frequency/amplitude, or tungsten sonotrode is given. A cited 1977 paper concerns W solubility in cupro-nickel melts.

contexts.context: The AMAZEMET-like patent describes ultrasonic atomization of conductive “heavy metals” (density >8500 kg/m³; liquidus >800°C), including copper and alloys, at ≤1000 mL/h, preferably <500 mL/h. Raw material melts in a pool on an electrically conductive sonotrode, which acts as the anode; a separate cooled, non-consumable tungsten electrode is the cathode. A 10–40 V arc melts the feed. Vacuum operation uses 0.0001–0.01 barA; gas operation uses inert gas at 0.01–6 barA (preferably 1–1.5 barA), with a 5–40 mm arc. Atomization temperature is typically ~1.3× melting temperature. No sonotrode material, frequency, amplitude, service life, erosion, or tungsten contamination data are provided.
contexts.question:
Has anyone used tungsten, a tungsten alloy (W-Re, W-La2O3, W-Ni-Fe or W-Ni-Cu heavy alloy) or a
tungsten-coated carbon or graphite part as an ultrasonic sonotrode, horn tip or atomizing plate in
contact with molten metal, especially copper, nickel or copper-nickel alloys (for example in an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another ultrasonic atomizer, or in ultrasonic melt treatment)? If so, report the
melt, temperature, frequency and amplitude, how long the part lasted, how much it eroded or dissolved,
and how much W ended up in the product. If not, give the closest precedents: W or W-coated parts in
contact with molten Cu or Ni alloys (crucibles, nozzles, thermocouple sheaths, casting molds), and Mo
or Nb sonotrodes used with Cu or Ni melts.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes an ultrasonic heavy-metal atomizer tested for platinum, silver, palladium, gold, and copper alloys. It uses a cooled sonotrode operating at **35 kHz**; atomization requires hot-end vibration velocity **Vs ≥ 0.2 m/s**, with **Vs = 2πfUs**, and transducer power at least **30 W/cm²** of molten-pool area. Argon enters at **293 K**; an electric arc rated **1,200–8,200 W** melts feedstock. A **3-mm non-consumable tungsten electrode tip** serves as the cathode/arc electrode, while the sonotrode is the anode. No sonotrode material, melt temperature, service life, erosion, or tungsten contamination is reported.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports an unambiguous tungsten–copper molten-contact experiment, but it does not provide data for tungsten dissolving in Cu–Ni melts, nor does it cite or discuss Eremenko, Minakova, and Churakov (1977). Tungsten microlattices were first thermally processed and sintered at 1200, 1300, or 1400 °C. For copper infiltration, the sintered W lattices were placed in an alumina crucible, covered with approximately equal-volume copper, heated under vacuum to either 1200 or 1300 °C—both above copper’s 1085 °C melting point—and held for 60 minutes. Excess copper was subsequently removed mechanically until the tungsten struts were exposed. These conditions establish durations and temperatures for Cu–W exposure, but the excerpt gives no measured tungsten mass loss, dissolution rate, interfacial recession, coating performance, sheath behavior, or quantitative composition change. Nickel appears only as a small NiO ink additive, with the printed lattice caption specifying 0.5 wt% Ni; this is not evidence of a molten Ni-containing alloy contact test. The article’s stated objective was fabrication of architectured W–Cu composites by liquid-copper infiltration rather than measurement of W solubility or protective Ni-alloy coatings.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not provide the experimental measurements from Eremenko, Minakova, and Churakov’s 1977 paper, but identifies it as the cited source titled “Solubility of tungsten in cupro-nickel melts” (Poroshk. Metall., No. 4, 53–58, 1977). It therefore provides a direct bibliographic lead for published tungsten dissolution data in Cu–Ni melts, but no Cu–Ni composition, exposure duration, temperature series, tungsten mass loss, dissolution depth, or protective-sheath/coating test results are reproduced here. The present paper instead measures tungsten dissolving in liquid nickel at 1525°C using rotating-disc specimens. For comparison with future Cu–Ni data, it reports solubility rate constants of approximately 0.77×10^-4 m/s at 4.45 rad/s, 1.57×10^-4 m/s at 16.7 rad/s, 1.95×10^-4 m/s at 25.0 rad/s, and 3.72×10^-4 m/s at 36.8 rad/s. The dependence K = (3.47 ± 0.04)×10^-5 ω^(0.58 ± 0.02) is interpreted as diffusion-controlled over 4.45–25 rad/s. The calculated diffusion coefficient of W in liquid Ni at 1525°C is (1.41 ± 0.07)×10^-8 m²/s. These are Ni-only measurements, not unambiguous Cu–W exposures or tests of W protective coatings or sheaths.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes tungsten-coated diamond particles used to fabricate diamond–copper composites, but it does not provide published measurements of tungsten dissolution in Cu–Ni melts, tested Ni-alloy molten-contact W coatings or sheaths, or quantitative tungsten loss. The reported processing route deposited an approximately 200 nm tungsten layer by pulsed magnetron sputtering, followed by vacuum annealing at 1100 °C for varying durations until the tungsten was converted to tungsten carbide. The annealing atmosphere was maintained at 5 × 10−4 Pa, with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Copper was subsequently chemically deposited over the metallized diamond, and the particles were consolidated by hot pressing. The article’s focus is interfacial tungsten-carbide structure and thermal conductivity in diamond–copper composites, rather than W–Cu–Ni compatibility or molten-metal corrosion. Although the excerpt mentions that the generated tungsten-carbide structures and their distribution require further elucidation, it gives no direct exposure duration for molten Cu or Cu–Ni, no measured dissolution rate, coating-loss value, residual W thickness, or Ni-alloy contact test. Thus, it may serve only as a peripheral reference for a W-derived carbide interlayer processed at 1100 °C, not as evidence for quantitative tungsten stability in Cu–Ni melts.

contexts.context: This excerpt is only indirectly relevant to the requested Cu-Ni/W literature. It reports measurements for tungsten dissolving in pure liquid nickel at 1525°C, not cupro-nickel melts, protective Ni-alloy coatings, W sheaths, or direct Cu-W exposures. Using stirred-melt experiments with rotating cylindrical monocrystalline tungsten specimens, the authors measured a tungsten solubility of 50.7 ± 1.4 wt.% (24.7 ± 0.7 at.%) at 1525°C. They found that the unstirred-melt value was approximately 4–5% lower than the stirred-melt value, attributing the discrepancy to concentration gradients in the unstirred liquid. Cylindrical specimens were immersed for 2–4 hours, and constant weight loss after 2, 3, and 4 hours indicated that equilibrium required no more than 2 hours. Separate rotating-disc tests examined solution rates at rotation rates of 4–37 rad/s and times of 270–720 seconds. Copper appears only as an analytical recovery medium: liquid copper was used to remove W–Ni alloy droplets from specimen ends, followed by acid dissolution. The excerpt therefore supplies useful benchmark values and experimental procedures for W/Ni dissolution, but it does not provide the requested Eremenko–Minakova–Churakov 1977 Cu-Ni data or unambiguous Cu-W exposure measurements.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report tungsten dissolution in Cu–Ni (cupro-nickel) melts, nor does it identify Eremenko, Minakova, or Churakov’s 1977 publication. It also contains no tested Ni-alloy molten-contact protective coating or tungsten sheath data, and no quantitative tungsten loss measurements for Cu–W exposures. The relevant material concerns tungsten solubility in liquid silver. It describes experimental sampling and analysis procedures, including dissolving tungsten crucibles away from silver in fused KOH/NaNO3, taking successive samples through the silver ingot, and comparing wet-chemistry with neutron-activation analyses. The report states that no significant concentration gradient was detected after quenching a 2380°C ingot. It gives estimated tungsten solubilities of 1.2 ppm at 2380°C and 0.7 ppm at 2200°C. It also notes agreement between results from bar-stock and vapor-deposited tungsten crucibles, potentially relevant as a methodological precedent for evaluating crucible or sheath compatibility, but not as evidence for Cu–Ni or Cu–W behavior. No exposure duration is provided for the silver solubility values in this excerpt.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports no ultrasonic sonotrode, horn, atomizer, erosion, lifetime, or tungsten pickup data. It studied liquid nickel (99.99% Ni and alloys) by constrained-drop surface-tension measurements at roughly 1723–1923 K. A tungsten–rhenium thermocouple measured temperature inside a molybdenum tube; the metal contacted a corundum (98% Al₂O₃ + TiO₂ binder) cup, not tungsten. Samples were held while photographing drops for up to 600 s, with temperatures increased in 10–15°C steps. Tested materials included Ni–Re alloys, including “Ni–6.7% Re–4% W–1% Mo–10% Co,” but no component durability or contamination results were given.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Has anyone used tungsten, a tungsten alloy (W-Re, W-La2O3, W-Ni-Fe or W-Ni-Cu heavy alloy) or a
tungsten-coated carbon or graphite part as an ultrasonic sonotrode, horn tip or atomizing plate in
contact with molten metal, especially copper, nickel or copper-nickel alloys (for example in an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another ultrasonic atomizer, or in ultrasonic melt treatment)? If so, report the
melt, temperature, frequency and amplitude, how long the part lasted, how much it eroded or dissolved,
and how much W ended up in the product. If not, give the closest precedents: W or W-coated parts in
contact with molten Cu or Ni alloys (crucibles, nozzles, thermocouple sheaths, casting molds), and Mo
or Nb sonotrodes used with Cu or Ni melts.


Yes. ## Finding

**Yes—but the documented tungsten sonotrode tip was used with a titanium alloy, not a copper or nickel melt.** A patent describes a technical-grade tungsten working tip that supports molten Ti7Al6Nb and transmits ultrasound. I found **no verified report of a tungsten, W–Re, W–La₂O₃, W–Ni–Fe or W–Ni–Cu tip, or a tungsten-coated carbon/graphite tip, operating against molten Cu, Ni or Cu–Ni** with measured service life, erosion and W pickup. This is a limit of the located evidence, not proof that no such equipment has ever been used. (US11938557B2 pages 7-10, US11938557B2 pages 16-18, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42, EP3766610A1 pages 2-8)

| Precedent and evidential status | Melt and conditions | Lifetime, loss and product contamination |
|---|---|---|
| **W tip, explicit patent embodiment:** [name redacted], *Sonotrode for processing of liquid metals*, US11938557B2. A 20-g, technical-grade W M8 working tip is attached to a Ti6Al4V sonotrode body and contacts the melt. | A **3-g Ti7Al6Nb** charge is melted with a **100-A plasma arc for 30 s**; the arc is then extinguished and ultrasound applied. The assembly’s frequency is **20,200 Hz measured at 297 K**—not a stated frequency measured at melt temperature—and tip amplitude is **10 µm**. Melt temperature and duration of subsequent sonication are **not given**. | **No quantified lifetime, recession, mass loss or W concentration** in the treated alloy. The patent contemplates replacing a tip after degradation, but supplies no wear measurement. This is a disclosed worked example, **not** a published Cu/Ni durability trial. (US11938557B2 pages 7-10, US11938557B2 pages 16-18) |
| **Mo tip, reported rePowder processing:** Goncharov *et al.*, *Metals* **16**, 318 (2026), doi:10.3390/met16030318. | An **AMAZEMET rePowder** with a **molybdenum sonotrode** atomizes an Al–Cr–Cu–Fe–Mn–Ni high-entropy-alloy feedstock prepared from elemental powders and arc-remelted rods. This is a **Cu- and Ni-containing alloy**, not pure Cu or a conventional Cu–Ni alloy. The accessible methods give **no atomization temperature, frequency or amplitude**; temperatures given for later WC–HEA sintering are not melt-atomization temperatures. | **No tip operating life, erosion/dissolution rate or W pickup** reported. The subsequent **WC–12 wt% HEA** mixture contains deliberately added WC and must not be interpreted as W contamination from the Mo sonotrode. (goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 2-4) |
| **CuNi3Si atomization, vibrating material unspecified:** Bielecki, US20240390977A1. | The patent expressly reports **CuNi3Si powder made at 35 kHz** using a cooled sonotrode in argon; it gives feedstock **liquidus 1348 K (≈1075 °C)**, **not a measured operating melt temperature**. Its tested apparatus has a **3-mm tungsten arc cathode separate from the vibrating sonotrode/anode**. It reports an experimental hot-end vibration-*velocity* threshold of **0.2 m/s peak**, not the actual displacement amplitude for this CuNi3Si run. | The patent says sonotrodes are exchanged when contaminated by a previous feedstock, but gives **neither tip composition nor service life, erosion or product W assay**. Thus its W electrode cannot establish a W sonotrode or W-derived powder contamination. (US20240390977A1 pages 38-40, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42) |
| **Nb-tip design, not a Cu/Ni performance test:** Kaczynski *et al.*, EP3766610A1. | An atomizing-sonotrode embodiment has a **niobium core pressed into a copper-alloy body**; W and Mo alloys are listed as *alternative* core materials. It describes possible installation for steels and Ti alloys, but gives **no identified Cu/Ni melt run, test temperature, measured frequency or amplitude** for its Nb embodiment. | **No measured life, wear or contamination.** The coating specified on the *coolant-side body* is for protection against cooling-liquid cavitation, not a W coating on graphite exposed to metal. (EP3766610A1 pages 1-2, EP3766610A1 pages 2-8) |
| **Nb immersed-sonotrode experiment, lower-temperature comparator:** Naydenkin *et al.*, *Metals* **7**, 544 (2017), doi:10.3390/met7120544. | **AA6082 aluminum alloy** at **730 °C**, **17.5 kHz**, approximately **30 µm** working amplitude. A niobium conical sonotrode was used for **1 min** of degassing and **2 additional min** after addition of Al–Al₂O₃ master alloy. | Three minutes describes **one treatment schedule, not demonstrated tip life**. Nb wear and pickup are not quantified. The alloy’s minor nominal Cu content does not make this a molten-copper trial. (naydenkin2017influenceofcombined pages 1-3) |

**Closest non-ultrasonic W–melt-contact evidence.** Pure Cu infiltrated W scaffolds at **1250 °C for 10 min** under argon in Han *et al.*; interfacial microscopy found distinct, bonded Cu and W constituents, but neither W loss nor W dissolved in the Cu was measured. Calvo *et al.* similarly infiltrated W microlattices with Cu at **1200 or 1300 °C for 60 min** in vacuum. These are stationary, short-duration composite-fabrication exposures—not qualifying crucible, nozzle, mold, sheath or cavitating-tip lifetime tests. (han2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-5, calvo2018microstructureandprocessing pages 2-3)

Nickel presents a particularly strong **chemical-dissolution warning**. Natanzon *et al.*, *Soviet Powder Metallurgy and Metal Ceramics* **31**, 161–165 (1992), doi:10.1007/BF00794054, measured **50.7 ± 1.4 wt% equilibrium W solubility in stirred liquid Ni at 1525 °C**; W specimens were immersed for **2–4 h** to establish equilibrium. Their rotating-disc tests measured dissolution over **270–720 s**, with solution-rate constants dependent on rotation. This is a deliberately dissolving stationary/rotating W specimen, **not an ultrasonic wear rate or a predicted W concentration in atomized powder**. That paper also cites Eremenko, Minakova and Churakov, “Solubility of tungsten in cupro-nickel melts,” *Poroshkovaya Metallurgiya*, no. 4, 53–58 (1977); I could verify the citation **but not obtain its Cu–Ni-specific numerical results**. (natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 1-2, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 2-4, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 4-5)

**Bottom line for the requested metrics:** The titanium-alloy patent supplies the sole located explicit molten-metal-contact **W vibrating-tip** configuration and its frequency/amplitude, but **not its melt temperature, tip life, loss or W pickup**. The Mo/rePowder paper and 35-kHz CuNi3Si patent establish substantially closer **Cu/Ni-containing ultrasonic-processing** precedents, but do **not** establish a W sonotrode or quantify its contamination. I found no defensible numerical W-in-product value or service-life estimate for a W, W-alloy or W-coated-graphite sonotrode in molten Cu/Ni; neither the short stationary Cu exposures nor Ni equilibrium solubility can be substituted for those measurements. (US11938557B2 pages 16-18, goncharov2026designofcobaltfree pages 2-4, US20240390977A1 pages 40-42, han2022mechanicalpropertiesof pages 2-5, natanzon1992solubilityandkinetics pages 1-2)

info.query:
Has anyone used tungsten, a tungsten alloy (W-Re, W-La2O3, W-Ni-Fe or W-Ni-Cu heavy alloy) or a
tungsten-coated carbon or graphite part as an ultrasonic sonotrode, horn tip or atomizing plate in
contact with molten metal, especially copper, nickel or copper-nickel alloys (for example in an
AMAZEMET rePOWDER or another ultrasonic atomizer, or in ultrasonic melt treatment)? If so, report the
melt, temperature, frequency and amplitude, how long the part lasted, how much it eroded or dissolved,
and how much W ended up in the product. If not, give the closest precedents: W or W-coated parts in
contact with molten Cu or Ni alloys (crucibles, nozzles, thermocouple sheaths, casting molds), and Mo
or Nb sonotrodes used with Cu or Ni melts.
